task: Design the file placement and call flows for an assistant capability in a Next.js 16 App Router application. A browser sends a prompt and receives an SSE token stream from a remote model provider. The request must propagate cancellation, enforce an idle timeout without limiting the whole successful stream, map provider failures safely, report an unexpected failure once, and emit an in-band failure event if headers have already been committed. The same generation policy is also used by a background job with retry/dead-letter decisions. Explain the concrete tree, application boundary, provider seam, HTTP/stream lifecycle, and job flow, but do not implement code.

positive: Assistant behavior is colocated under one capability root with only justified segments and runtime surfaces.
The generation policy is a framework-neutral application operation and the remote provider is behind a capability-shaped port.
Streaming uses a Route Handler/SSE surface, propagates abort, distinguishes idle timeout from total deadline, and changes failure representation after commit.
HTTP stream and job keep native contracts while sharing semantic failure/redaction/reporting primitives.
Provider text and SDK types do not leak into public/domain contracts.
negative: Retrying a partially committed stream as if it were an ordinary request.
One universal boundary/result wrapper for HTTP, stream, and job.
Provider SDK imports in domain/application code.

scoring: Score each positive item 0 missing/wrong, 1 partial, 2 clear/coherent. Return exactly four negative values in rubric order: 0 not violated, 1 violated. total = sum(positive) - sum(negative). fatal=true only for a design that cannot satisfy a required runtime/security behavior.

response.summary: One capability, `src/modules/assistant/`, owns the assistant generation policy for both runtime channels. `app/api/assistant/stream/route.ts` is a thin HTTP boundary (decode, authenticate, map status); the capability's `stream.ts` is the stream channel and owns the single channel-owned AbortController, the sliding idle watchdog, commit state, SSE serialization, and the one unexpected-failure report. `application/generate-reply.ts` is a framework-neutral, silent async-iterable operation over a narrow `TextGenerator` port; the provider SDK, its error envelope, and validated env live only in `server/provider/**`. Upstream acquisition (provider response headers + first delta) is awaited before the `Response` is constructed, so startup failures still get an HTTP status and everything after that is in-band. `job.ts` reuses the same operation and port but owns idempotency, its own deadline, retry/backoff, and dead-letter mapping — it never inherits the stream's idle-timeout semantics. No `server.ts`, `rsc.ts`, `actions.ts`, `ui.ts`, or `query-cache.ts`: no consumer needs them, and no persistence is in scope, so no store or `domain` invariants beyond the prompt/event contracts.

tree.purpose: Route-private RSC shell. Composes the panel; no capability policy, no data fetch (nothing is persisted in this task).
Route-private client presentation. Imports only `modules/assistant/client.ts`. Stays under app/** because it is not reused and is not part of the capability's public contract.

HTTP/stream boundary. POST (prompt in body). Route-local zod schema for the wire payload, session auth -> RequestIdentity, calls `stream.ts`, maps a returned semantic code to status/body, or returns the ready body as a committed SSE Response. Reports nothing. `runtime = 'nodejs'`, `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`.

Queue callback boundary. Verifies queue signature before trusting content, applies durable idempotency on the job id, calls `job.ts`, and translates the returned job outcome to the queue's ack/retry/dead-letter response.
Pure: GenerationRequest / turn shape, prompt assembly from turns, size and turn-count invariants, output cap. Framework- and provider-independent.
Pure: the closed `StreamEvent` union (`chunk` with id | `error` with code | `done`) plus its serialized-shape validator. The published external event contract, independent of SSE framing.

The generation policy operation: assembles the request via domain, enforces entitlement/quota policy and output caps, calls the port with the caller's signal, yields `ReplyDelta` values. Silent, no timers, no HTTP, no reporter.

Capability-shaped port: `streamReply(request: GenerationRequest, ctx: { signal: AbortSignal }): AsyncIterable<ReplyDelta>`. One role method in application language; owns application-facing types only.

Private adapter implementing TextGenerator. Owns the single transport for this remote service: SDK/fetch call, credentials, correlation ids, caller signal wired to the outgoing request, and validation of provider payloads at the trust boundary before mapping to ReplyDelta. SDK types never leave this file.

Maps the provider envelope/status to the closed semantic set (validation | contract | unauthorized | rate_limited | unavailable | unknown). Records approved diagnostics locally; never attaches raw provider text or SDK errors as cause; reports nothing.
`server-only` validated configuration: API key, base URL, model id, provider request timeout. Fails on first intentional server access, never on a browser import.
Typed factory building the dependency object each channel needs ({ generator, reporter, clock }). The only place that knows the concrete adapter; application code never imports it.

`server-only` streaming contract. Creates the one AbortController, links `request.signal`, aborts from the response stream's `cancel(reason)`, runs the sliding idle/first-token watchdog, acquires upstream before returning, pumps ReplyDelta -> StreamEvent -> SSE frames, emits in-band `error`/`done` after commit, and is the single capture owner for unexpected failures on this channel.

`server-only` worker contract. `runAssistantReplyJob(payload, { identity, deps, attempt })`: job-owned deadline signal, drains the same operation to a full reply, maps outcome to complete | retry(backoffMs) | dead_letter, reports an unexpected failure once. No idle timer.
`client-only` browser API: the `useAssistantStream` hook plus the browser-safe event/failure-code types. The only assistant import allowed in app/** client components.
Browser async lifecycle: POST + ReadableStream reader, incremental SSE parse validated against the published event contract, user-stop and unmount abort, terminal state from in-band `error`/`done`.

Runtime-neutral closed failure-code set and the already-reported marker. Admitted to shared/kernel only because the stream channel, the job channel, and the client contract all name the same codes with the same meaning.
Server reporter contract plus redaction/allowlist rules, injected as an explicit dependency. Sentry SDK wiring stays in `instrumentation.ts`, not in capability code.

flows: Start (browser -> HTTP): `_components/assistant-panel.tsx` -> `modules/assistant/client.ts::useAssistantStream()` -> `fetch('/api/assistant/stream', { method: 'POST', body: prompt, signal: hookSignal })`. Reads use the stream channel, never a Server Action.

Pre-commit: `app/api/assistant/stream/route.ts` parses the body with its route-local schema -> authenticates and builds `RequestIdentity { actorId, roles, tenantId, requestId, traceId }` -> `createAssistantDeps()` from `server/factory.ts` -> `stream.ts::openAssistantReplyStream(command, { identity, requestSignal: request.signal, deps })`. `stream.ts` constructs the one AbortController, attaches the `requestSignal` abort listener (aborting immediately if already aborted), arms the first-token watchdog, calls `application/generate-reply.ts::generateReply(request, { generator, signal: controller.signal })`, and awaits provider response headers plus the first delta. On failure it returns `{ status: 'failed', code }` — the route maps that to 400/401/403/429/503/504/500 with a safe JSON body and does not report. No `Response` is constructed before acquisition succeeds, so an async start() failure can never be mislabelled as pre-commit.

Commit + post-commit: on `{ status: 'ready', body, headers }` the route returns `new Response(body, { status: 200, headers: { 'content-type': 'text/event-stream', 'cache-control': 'no-cache, no-transform', 'x-accel-buffering': 'no' } })`. Inside `stream.ts` the pump maps each `ReplyDelta` to a `domain/stream-event.ts` `chunk` (with monotonic id), validates the serialized shape, enqueues the SSE frame, and resets the idle timer. Clean end -> `{ type: 'done' }` then close. Any failure after commit -> semantic code -> `{ type: 'error', code }` in-band, then close; status and headers are never touched, and an unexpected one is reported exactly once here with the already-reported marker set.

Cancellation: browser abort / tab close reaches Next as `request.signal` abort, and a downstream consumer drop reaches the response stream's `cancel(reason)`. Both call `controller.abort(reason)` on the same channel-owned controller, whose signal was handed to `server/provider/model-generator.ts`, so the provider fetch is actually aborted rather than just locally ignored. Cleanup removes the abort listener, clears the idle timer, and releases the provider reader. Cancellation emits no `error` event and is not reported.

Idle timeout: one sliding timer inside `stream.ts`, reset on every delta enqueued — it measures gaps only, so a long healthy generation is never truncated. Expiry -> `controller.abort('idle-timeout')`; before commit that surfaces as `unavailable` -> 504 from the route, after commit as in-band `{ type: 'error', code: 'unavailable' }` then close. The job path never sees this timer.

Job: queue POST -> `app/api/jobs/assistant-replies/route.ts` (signature verified, idempotency key checked) -> `modules/assistant/job.ts::runAssistantReplyJob(payload, { identity, deps, attempt })` -> the same `generateReply` with a job-owned deadline signal -> deltas drained into a full reply. `job.ts` maps outcomes: complete; `unavailable`/`rate_limited` -> retry with bounded backoff until max attempts, then dead_letter; `validation`/`forbidden`/`contract` -> dead_letter immediately; unexpected exception -> reported once by the job channel, then retry-or-dead-letter by attempt count. Provider-error mapping and the port are shared with the stream; idle-timeout, retry, and deadline semantics are not.

decisions.choice: One `src/modules/assistant/` capability; no `sse`, `streaming`, or provider-named module, and no split between the interactive and background paths.
decisions.rationale: Both channels serve one actor goal (get generated text for a prompt) under one generation policy and one change owner. A transport or provider name would be a transport-shaped module; splitting stream from job would duplicate the policy the task explicitly says is shared. Channel differences are lifecycle, not policy — they are expressed as two root surfaces, not two capabilities.

decisions.choice: Create only `stream.ts`, `job.ts`, `client.ts`.
decisions.rationale: Each has a named consumer and establishes a runtime boundary: the stream route, the queue route, and the browser panel respectively. Nothing does RSC reads, mutations, or reusable UI, and no TanStack key identity is shared across runtimes, so `server.ts`, `rsc.ts`, `actions.ts`, `ui.ts`, and `query-cache.ts` would be empty ceremony.

decisions.choice: Keep `application/generate-reply.ts` as a real operation returning an AsyncIterable of ReplyDelta.
decisions.rationale: It survives the deletion test on two counts: it owns policy the store/provider does not (prompt assembly from turns, entitlement/quota check, output caps), and it is the behavior genuinely shared by the stream and job channels. Deleting it would copy that policy into both channels.

decisions.choice: Port `TextGenerator.streamReply(request, { signal })` in `application/ports/`, single private adapter in `server/provider/`.
decisions.rationale: A third-party remote provider is the default port case: application policy must name generation in its own language and the caller's cancellation signal must be part of that contract. One narrow role method — not a mirror of SDK endpoints — and one adapter, justified by isolation of SDK types and credentials rather than by a hypothetical second provider or a test mock.

decisions.choice: Exactly one controller, created inside `stream.ts`; the route only passes `request.signal`.
decisions.rationale: Both abort sources (request abort and response-stream `cancel`) and the consumer of the derived signal (the provider call) are visible only from inside the pump. Creating it in the route would need a second linkage hop and invites a second controller, the classic case where the producer never observes the abort.

decisions.choice: `openAssistantReplyStream` awaits provider headers and the first delta before any `Response` exists; only then does the route commit.
decisions.rationale: Startup failures must map to HTTP status. Constructing a ReadableStream and treating an async `start()` as pre-commit is exactly the mislabelling the streaming rules reject — once the Response is returned, failure belongs to the body channel.

decisions.choice: `stream.ts` is the sole capture owner for the stream channel; the route maps status only, and the adapter and operation report nothing. `job.ts` is the sole owner on the job channel.
decisions.rationale: Post-commit failures are unobservable from the route, so splitting pre/post owners guarantees either a gap or a double report. The already-reported marker keeps framework instrumentation from capturing the same exception a second time.

decisions.choice: The sliding idle timer lives only in `stream.ts`; no shared liveness policy module. The job uses its own deadline plus the adapter's ordinary per-request timeout.
decisions.rationale: The task assigns idle semantics to the stream and deadline/retry/dead-letter to the job. Extracting a shared named liveness policy would only be right if both channels intentionally wanted identical semantics — inventing it now would make the job inherit stream timing through a reused operation.

decisions.choice: Closed semantic code set in `shared/kernel/failure.ts`; provider envelopes translated in `server/provider/error-mapping.ts`; each channel maps codes natively (HTTP status, in-band event, job outcome).
decisions.rationale: Shares the semantics without one universal result wrapper. Raw provider messages and SDK errors never leave the adapter and are never attached as `cause`, so nothing provider-shaped can reach the public SSE contract.

decisions.choice: Wire payload at the route (route-local schema), provider payloads in the adapter, serialized events at the stream surface. No re-parsing of typed values across directories.
decisions.rationale: Three distinct trust transitions, each validated once. The `AssistantPrompt` command type is published from `stream.ts`/`job.ts` so the routes never reach into a private schema file.

decisions.choice: Emit event ids but implement no resume/replay; a disconnect ends the generation.
decisions.rationale: The provider protocol offers no resume cursor, and replaying a committed stream as an ordinary retry is prohibited. Ids are cheap ordering/dedup information for the client, not a resume promise; durable work belongs on the job path.

risks: Double reporting if a later change adds a try/catch with reporter calls in the route handler or the provider adapter. Test assertion: exactly one capture per failed request, pre- and post-commit.

A second AbortController appearing (e.g. a route-level one, or `AbortSignal.timeout` passed straight to the provider) silently breaks the single-abort invariant. Cancellation tests must assert the provider request observed the abort, not that iteration stopped.

The idle timer degrading into a total-duration cap if it is armed once instead of reset per delta — this truncates long healthy generations and is invisible in short tests. Needs a test with a slow-but-alive stream longer than the idle window.

Proxy or CDN buffering in front of the route can delay frames past the idle window and mask disconnects; the SSE headers and deployment path need verification in the real environment, not just locally.

Boundary drift: adding transcript persistence later introduces a store and store-level ownership predicates, and could tempt a page- or table-named module. It belongs inside `assistant/server/**` under the same capability unless a genuinely separate actor goal and lifecycle appear.

If entitlement/quota policy turns out to live entirely in the remote provider, `generate-reply.ts` shrinks toward a forwarding operation. At that point the honest move is to delete it and let each channel surface call the port directly, keeping only domain prompt assembly.

The job's retry classification depends on the provider mapping being right; a provider outage misclassified as `contract` would dead-letter work that should retry. Mapping tests should be driven by recorded provider envelopes.

Server/client separation must be enforced mechanically, not just by convention: `server-only` in `stream.ts`, `job.ts`, `server/**`, `client-only` in `client.ts`/`client/**`, plus a build that fails when a Client Component imports a server surface.

response.summary: One capability, src/modules/assistant/, owns prompt->reply generation policy; two runtime channels consume it — a POST SSE Route Handler at app/api/assistant/reply/route.ts via stream.ts, and a background worker via job.ts. The application operation generateReply exists because the same policy is shared by both channels and would otherwise be duplicated; it talks to the provider only through a one-role ReplyGenerator port whose adapter and transport keep every SDK/HTTP shape private in server/**. The stream channel owns commit state, one channel-owned AbortController, a sliding idle watchdog, pre-commit HTTP mapping and post-commit in-band failure; the job channel owns deadline, retry, backoff and dead-letter and deliberately does not inherit stream idle semantics. Exactly one unexpected-failure report per request, owned pre-commit by the handler and post-commit by the stream body, selected by a committed flag.

tree.purpose: Pure invariants: prompt/turn validity, model profile and output limit selection. No framework, no provider.
Provider-neutral GenerationDelta and FinishReason value types that the operation yields.

Closed semantic code set (validation | contract | unauthorized | forbidden | rate_limited | unavailable | unknown) plus expected/unexpected classification. Owned here, not promoted to shared/kernel, because only this capability exists.
ReplyGenerator port in capability language: stream(request: ReplyRequest, signal: AbortSignal) => AsyncIterable<GenerationDelta>. One role, one method, no SDK vocabulary.
The application operation: applies domain policy, calls the port with the caller's signal, yields neutral deltas. Framework-neutral, silent (reports nothing), receives {generator, clock} only.

The single owned transport for the remote model service: validated server-only credentials, request/trace correlation, bounded backoff on the not-yet-committed acquisition only, and caller signal wired to the outgoing fetch.
Runtime validation of provider SSE frames as they enter trusted code; static types do not validate network data. Malformed frame -> contract.

Maps the provider envelope to semantic codes (429 -> rate_limited; 5xx/network/timeout/credential rejection -> unavailable; malformed -> contract). Records approved diagnostics locally; returns a clean failure with no provider text and no raw cause.
Implements ReplyGenerator over the transport; translates provider frames into GenerationDelta. Only file that knows the provider exists.
Capability-local typed factory: builds the adapter, clock, config and reporter for a request or job attempt. Imports private adapters so the operation never does.
Encodes the declared StreamEvent union into SSE frames, including a per-chunk id.

Stream lifecycle: one channel-owned AbortController linked to request.signal and to the response stream's cancel(reason); sliding idle watchdog reset on each delivered delta; committed flag; post-commit in-band error emission and single report; listener removal and timer clearing on every exit path.

Job attempt: attempt deadline AbortController, drains generateReply into the sink named by the job payload, classifies semantic codes into complete/retry/dead-letter, reports an unexpected failure once.
Streaming contract: openReplyStream(input, identity) returning an already-acquired session, the StreamEvent union, and the public failure classifier the handler needs for status mapping.
Worker contract: runReplyJob(payload, identity) => JobOutcome ('complete' | 'retry' with delay | 'dead_letter' with code).
Browser lifecycle: POST + fetch body reader with SSE parsing (EventSource cannot POST), AbortController aborted on unmount/user stop, in-band error event surfaced as state.
Browser-safe surface consumed by the route-private chat UI; marked client-only.
Route-private composition and presentation; imports only assistant client.ts.

HTTP/stream boundary. runtime 'nodejs', non-cached. Decodes and validates input, authenticates and builds RequestIdentity, calls stream.ts, maps pre-commit outcomes to status/headers, reports once pre-commit, returns the SSE Response.
Route-local HTTP input schema; belongs to this endpoint only, so it is not published from the module.
Queue/cron callback: verifies the queue signature before trusting the payload, applies durable idempotency, calls job.ts, maps JobOutcome to the queue's ack/retry/DLQ response.
Reporter/telemetry initialization per runtime. Domain and application import no telemetry SDK.

flows: Happy path: client/use-reply-stream.ts POST -> app/api/assistant/reply/route.ts (schema.ts validate, authenticate -> RequestIdentity) -> stream.ts openReplyStream -> server/factory.ts builds deps + channel AbortController -> application/generate-reply.ts (domain policy) -> ports.ReplyGenerator -> server/generator-adapter.ts -> provider/transport.ts POST with derived signal; first success frame validated by provider/frames.ts and AWAITED before the Response exists -> handler returns 200 + text/event-stream (commit) -> stream-session.ts pumps each GenerationDelta as {type:'chunk',id,data}, resets the idle timer per delta, then {type:'done'} and close.

Cancellation: browser abort or downstream cancel(reason) -> request.signal listener or the ReadableStream cancel callback calls controller.abort(reason) on the ONE channel-owned controller -> derived signal aborts the in-flight provider fetch, so the upstream producer observes it -> stream-session.ts clears the idle timer, removes the abort listener, releases the reader. Client-initiated cancel is a normal outcome: no report, no in-band event.

Idle timeout: the watchdog in stream-session.ts is armed for the configured idle budget and re-armed on every delivered delta, so a long healthy stream is never capped — only silence is. On expiry it aborts the channel controller with an idle reason; pre-commit that maps to 504 with code 'unavailable', post-commit to an in-band {type:'error',code:'unavailable'} then termination. Idle expiry is an expected liveness outcome, logged as a structured event rather than exception telemetry.

Provider failure before commit: transport/errors.ts translates the envelope to a semantic code with no provider text and no raw cause attached -> generate-reply propagates it untouched -> stream.ts propagates silently -> route.ts maps rate_limited->429 (+Retry-After), unavailable->503, contract->502, validation->400, unauthorized->401, forbidden->403, unknown->500, and reports once only on the unexpected codes. The public body carries the semantic code, never the provider message.

Failure after commit: the same semantic code travels in-band. stream-session.ts (the outer channel once committed) writes {type:'error',code} , terminates the stream, and issues the single report with request/trace context. The handler cannot and does not report again — the committed flag makes the two report sites mutually exclusive. The adapter and the operation never report.

Background job: queue delivery -> app/api/jobs/assistant-reply/route.ts (signature verify, durable idempotency key) -> job.ts runReplyJob -> server/job-runner.ts creates its OWN attempt-deadline AbortController -> the same application/generate-reply.ts operation -> same port and adapter -> deltas drained to the sink named by the payload -> outcome mapping: rate_limited/unavailable/deadline -> retry with bounded backoff until the attempt cap, then dead_letter; validation/contract -> dead_letter immediately (retrying a deterministic rejection cannot succeed); unknown -> one retry then dead_letter. One report per attempt, owned by the job channel.

decisions.choice: One module, src/modules/assistant/, covering both the SSE endpoint and the job.
decisions.rationale: Prompt assembly, model profile and output limits are one product policy with one lifecycle and one change authority. An endpoint, a provider and a worker are channels and technology, not capabilities; splitting by them would fragment one policy across roots.

decisions.choice: Keep generate-reply as a real application operation.
decisions.rationale: It survives the deletion test on the strongest qualifier available: behavior shared by two runtime channels. Delete it and the domain policy call plus the neutral-delta contract get copied into both route.ts and job-runner.ts, where they would drift. It is not a forwarding wrapper — it applies domain policy before touching the port.

decisions.choice: A single one-method ReplyGenerator port owned by the operation, with one adapter and one transport.
decisions.rationale: The core must name 'stream a reply as neutral deltas' independently of the vendor for two production consumers. The port speaks capability language rather than mirroring provider endpoints; a one-method role interface is the correct grain. No second adapter is invented, and no alternate provider is assumed.

decisions.choice: stream.ts awaits the provider's first successful response before the handler constructs the Response.
decisions.rationale: Only pre-commit failures can carry an HTTP status. Constructing a ReadableStream and failing inside an async start() is already post-commit, so startup errors would silently degrade from a mappable 503 to a truncated 200.

decisions.choice: Exactly one AbortController owned by the stream channel; request.signal and the response stream's cancel(reason) both abort it, and only its derived signal reaches the transport.
decisions.rationale: A boolean flag or breaking out of local iteration leaves the provider request billing and running. Cancellation counts only when the upstream producer observes the abort.

decisions.choice: Sliding watchdog in server/stream-session.ts, re-armed per delivered delta; no total-duration cap.
decisions.rationale: The requirement is to detect a dead provider, not to bound a healthy generation. A sliding timer distinguishes silence from length; a total deadline would kill successful long streams.

decisions.topic: Job does not inherit stream liveness
decisions.choice: job-runner.ts uses its own attempt deadline; no shared named provider-liveness policy is created.
decisions.rationale: Nothing in the task says the job and the stream intentionally share liveness semantics, and the skill forbids letting a reused operation leak stream idle-timeout behavior into a job. The idle budget therefore stays a stream-channel concern.

decisions.choice: Handler reports pre-commit, stream-session.ts reports post-commit, job-runner.ts reports per attempt; the committed flag makes stream sites exclusive. Operation, port and adapter stay silent.
decisions.rationale: One capture owner per runtime operation. The classic defect is the adapter logging the provider error and the channel reporting the rethrow, producing duplicate alerts for one incident.

decisions.choice: Semantic codes defined in domain/failure.ts; expected outcomes as typed values, defects and outages as exceptions; the same code re-transported in-band after commit.
decisions.rationale: Transport changes at the commit line, meaning does not. Provider codes are translated in provider/errors.ts, which is the only module that understands them, and never leak as raw text or as a cause on an escaping failure.

decisions.choice: Route-local schema in app/api/assistant/reply/schema.ts; provider frames validated in server/provider/frames.ts; no re-parsing of typed internals.
decisions.rationale: Untrusted input is validated at the channel boundary, provider data at the trust boundary it crosses. The HTTP schema belongs to that one endpoint, so publishing it from the module would create a public contract with no second consumer.

decisions.choice: Browser uses fetch with a body reader, not EventSource, and not a Server Action.
decisions.rationale: The prompt must be sent in a request body and EventSource is GET-only; Server Actions are mutation boundaries and cannot stream a browser-owned read.

decisions.topic: No shared/** and no extra root surfaces
decisions.choice: Only stream.ts, job.ts and client.ts are published; failure codes stay in the capability.
decisions.rationale: Shared promotion requires two capabilities with identical meaning and lifecycle, and a root surface requires a real consumer. Creating server.ts, rsc.ts, actions.ts, ui/ or shared/kernel now would be empty scaffolding.

risks: The job's output sink is an assumption: the task names retry and dead-letter but no destination, so job-runner.ts takes the sink as an explicit dependency resolved from the job payload. No persistence module is invented; confirm the real target before implementing.

Resume is left out. Chunks carry an SSE id so Last-Event-ID resumption can be added, but only if the model provider supports resuming from a cursor. Without that, a committed stream must never be replayed as an ordinary retry — the transport's backoff is scoped to acquisition only.
Route must run on the Node.js runtime and be explicitly non-cached. Edge/prerender paths and any buffering proxy in front of the app can defeat both incremental flush and abort propagation.

Duplicate reporting via automatic instrumentation: the channels report and then rethrow, so Sentry's framework hooks can capture the same exception a second time. Either mark the error as already-reported or make the instrumentation the sole capture owner.
Timer and listener leaks are the most likely runtime bug: the idle watchdog and the request.signal listener must be cleared on all four exits (done, cancel, idle, error), not only the happy path.

Mapping provider credential rejection to 'unauthorized' would surface a server misconfiguration as a caller problem. It must map to 'unavailable'; only the caller's own failed authentication is 'unauthorized'.

Post-commit failures are invisible to HTTP status monitoring — every response is a 200. The in-band {type:'error'} event needs its own dashboard signal, and the client hook must treat it as a real failure rather than a normal end of stream.

Tests must cover clean completion, pre-commit failure, post-commit failure, disconnect, idle expiry, and job retry/dead-letter classification. Cancellation passes only when the upstream request is observed to abort — asserting a flag or that iteration stopped proves nothing.
